topic.name: Writing an Infinite Geometric Series in Sigma Notation

exampleAnswers.title: Expressing an Infinite Series Using Sigma Notation Given The First Few Terms

question.text: Express the sum to infinity of the following geometric series using sigma notation: \[ 2+1+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}+\cdots \]
question.explanation:
The first term is $a_1 =2 $ and the second term is $a_2 =1.$ Using these two terms, we compute the common ratio:

\begin{align*} r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, the general term can be expressed as

\begin{align} a_n &= a_1\left(r\right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] &=2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}\\[5pt] &= 2 \left(\dfrac{2}{1} \right) \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}\\[5pt] &= 4 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n} . \end{align}

Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as \begin{align*} 2+1+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}+ \cdots & = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \\[5pt] & = \sum_{n=1}^\infty 4 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n} . \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing an Infinite Series Using Sigma Notation Given The First Few Terms

question.text: Write the following series in sigma notation in terms of index $n.$
question.explanation:
The first term is $a_1 = 5$ and the second term is $a_2 = -\dfrac{5}{3}.$ Using these two terms, we compute the common ratio:

\[ r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{5}{3}\right)}{5}=-\dfrac{1}{3} \]

Therefore, the general term can be expressed as

\begin{align} a_n &= a_1\left(r\right)^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 5 \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] &= 5 \left(-\dfrac{1}{3} \right)^{-1} \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\\[5pt] &= 5 \left(-3 \right) \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\\[5pt] &= (-15)\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}. \end{align}

Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as \begin{align*} 5 - \dfrac{5}{3}+\dfrac{5}{9}+ \cdots & = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \\[5pt] &= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{(-15)\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Expressing an Infinite Series Using Sigma Notation Given Its First Term and Common Ratio

question.text: Consider the sequence starting from $a_1=9$  with the property $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{1}{3}$ for all $n\geq 1.$ Write the sum to infinity $S$ of the terms of this series using sigma notation in terms of index $n.$
question.explanation:
Notice that the sequence is a geometric sequence since the ratio of any two successive terms is constant.

The first term of the sequence is $a_1 = 9,$ and the common ratio is $$ r = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \dfrac{1}{3}. $$

Therefore, the general term $a_n$ can be expressed as

\begin{align} a_n &= a_1\left(r\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] &= 9\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] &= 9\left(\frac{1}{3} \right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n}\\[5pt] &= 27\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n}. \end{align}

Finally, the infinite geometric series $S$ can be written in sigma notation as \begin{align*} S= \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n & = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{27\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the sequence starting from $a_1=2$ with the property $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{1}{5}$ for all $n\geq 1.$ Write the sum to infinity $S$ of the terms of this sequence using sigma notation in terms of index $n.$
question.explanation:
Notice that the sequence is a geometric sequence since the ratio of any two successive terms is constant.

The first term of the sequence is $a_1 = 2,$ and the common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \dfrac{1}{5}. \]

Therefore, the general term $a_n$ can be expressed as

\begin{align} a_n &= a_1\left(r\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] &= 2\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] &= 2\left(\frac{1}{5} \right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n}\\[5pt] &= 10\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n}. \end{align}

Finally, the infinite geometric series $S$ can be written in sigma notation as \begin{align*} S=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n & = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{10\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n}}. \end{align*}
